analysis.one_liner: Requires households earning over $1 million to pay at least 30% of income in federal taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 17 Senate sponsors and cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a 30% minimum tax on adjusted gross income above $1 million (the 'Buffett Rule'), after subtracting charitable donations and crediting taxes already paid, including payroll taxes. It would apply to tax years starting after 2015, adjust the $1 million threshold for inflation, and cut the deficit by billions per year, according to its findings. It was introduced in January 2015, sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and never advanced further before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the main beneficiary would be the federal Treasury — the bill's stated aim is to cut the deficit by billions of dollars a year by ensuring that the roughly 0.2% of taxpayers earning over $1 million pay at least a 30% effective rate, which everyone who pays taxes or depends on federal programs has a stake in. The bill also preserves charitable deductions and credits already-paid payroll taxes, so the tax only reaches income above what donors give away.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a minimum 30% tax rate on adjusted gross income above $1 million, so top earners cannot pay a lower effective rate through deductions and lower rates on investment income.
Counts payroll taxes and the alternative minimum tax toward the 30% floor and preserves charitable contribution deductions, so the tax targets only income above what is already given to charity.
States the goal of cutting the federal deficit by billions of dollars a year as an interim step toward broader tax reform closing loopholes for the wealthiest taxpayers.
Adjusts the $1 million threshold for inflation so the tax does not gradually capture middle-income earners over time.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals with adjusted gross income over $1 million — less than 1% of taxpayers — who would owe the difference between their current tax bill and the 30% floor. The bill is nonpartisan-scored as raising revenue, so the cost falls on high-income households while the deficit reduction accrues to everyone.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not address the underlying tax code structure; it adds a new parallel minimum tax on top of the existing alternative minimum tax, which the bill itself acknowledges is an interim measure pending comprehensive tax reform.

A 30% minimum rate applied above $1 million, even after charitable deductions, could reduce incentives for investment and charitable giving among affected taxpayers, an objection commonly raised against minimum-tax proposals of this type.
The tax applies only to non-corporate taxpayers, so it does not directly reach corporations, and the bill's revenue estimate is not provided in the text itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a small group of very high earners and preserves charitable deductions and credit for taxes paid, so its direct cost to most taxpayers is zero and the revenue goes toward deficit reduction. Its weakness is design: it is a floor layered on top of an already complex tax code rather than the comprehensive loophole-closing reform it says should follow, and the strongest good-faith objection is that a high minimum rate may blunt incentives for the taxpayers it reaches.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Finance Committee after being referred on the day it was introduced; the committee never acted on it and it never came up for a vote before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the Paying a Fair Share Act of 2015 on January 13, 2015, with 16 cosponsors (15 Democrats and one Independent).
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance on the same day it was introduced.
No further action was taken on the bill in the 114th Congress — it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote.
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, killing the bill under the rule that legislation does not carry over between Congresses.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households earning over $1 million are better off, since they avoided the 30% minimum tax; no other group gained anything from the bill dying, as the deficit reduction it would have produced never materialized.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Million-dollar earners who kept the status quo

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its sponsorship.

for.name: 16 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Baldwin, Durbin, Franken, Warren, Merkley, Sanders, Boxer, Markey, Reid, and Klobuchar.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 13, 2015 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Sen. Sanders; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-controlled Senate Finance Committee did not advance it.

industries.note: These taxpayers, less than 1% of filers, would owe the difference between their current tax bill and a 30% minimum rate. Their gain from the bill dying is the continuation of lower effective rates on investment income and deductions.

The bill preserves a charitable contribution deduction from the minimum tax calculation, so large donors to charity would not see that giving taxed away; the bill was designed to avoid discouraging donations.
